title: The services page an architecture studio actually needs
metaTitle: The services page an architecture studio needs
excerpt: List each commission in the client's words, with an outcome, a boundary, and a way to start a project. A grid of vague capabilities does not help them choose.
alt: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table, the moment a practice explains what it actually takes on.
caption: Explaining the work in the room, before it becomes a menu of slogans. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an architecture practice list as services?
faqs.answer: List the commissions a client can hire: a new house, an alteration, an interior, advice before a purchase, or whatever you truly take. Each one needs an outcome, a boundary, and a way to start a project conversation. Lines such as design excellence or spatial strategy can come off the page.

faqs.question: Does every service need its own page?
faqs.answer: Give a separate page to an offer that has its own boundary and its own kind of client. Keep a short section on the main list when the offer is real but rare. A page with no projects behind it, and no clear next step, is a heading in search of a practice.

faqs.question: What is the next step on each offer?
faqs.answer: The same action you use everywhere else: start a project conversation, with a note on what to send for that kind of job. An alteration wants the address and a note on what is failing, and advice before a purchase wants the listing and the timing. The form can stay short.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
An architecture studio services page should list the work in the client's language. Someone judging taste before competence needs each offer to carry an outcome, a boundary, and a next step: start a project conversation. A grid of vague capabilities does not help them choose.

Name the commissions you want. A new house. An alteration. An interior. Advice before someone buys a site. If a line could be copied onto any practice's website and still sound plausible, it is not a service yet. It is a mood.

## Write the offer in their words

Clients do not arrive saying they need a spatial narrative. They arrive with a terrace house that cannot fit a second child, a block they might buy, or a room that overheats. The page should meet those sentences. Your internal language can stay in the studio. The headings on this page are for the person with the site.

[Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for titles that are descriptive and concise, and for a main heading that makes the page obvious. "What we do" fails that test. "Alterations and extensions" passes it. "Houses on tight urban sites" passes it if that is truly the work. The heading is the offer. The paragraph underneath can add the limit.

[Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether the main heading is a useful summary, and whether a reader leaves able to act. A services page written for other architects, full of words they enjoy and clients do not use, fails both. Write the line you want a client to repeat to their partner: "They do alterations, and they will tell us if the lane house is the wrong job."

Read your current list out loud and mark every phrase you would not say in the first meeting. Those phrases are the edit. Replace each one with the building type, the scale, or the moment in the project when you are hired.

## Outcome, boundary, and the next step

Every offer on the page needs the same three parts. Skip one and the line collapses back into a capability.

The outcome is what the client has at the end of that scope. A planning set. A house they can build. A measured look at a property before they bid. A room that works for how they cook and sleep. Name the artifact or the change in their life. "A holistic design journey" is not an outcome.

The boundary is what you will not do inside that fee or that commission. You might design the house and not the loose furniture. You might take the alteration and not the neighboring development. You might advise on a purchase and stop before documentation. Boundaries are how a taste-led client learns that you are careful, not merely stylish. A practice with no edges looks like it will say yes and then struggle.

The next step is always the project conversation, worded for that offer. The header can say "Start a project." The paragraph can say what to include for this kind of job. An address and a note on what is failing, for an alteration. A listing link and a deadline, for advice before a purchase. The action is the same. The preparation is specific.

Use a repeated pattern so the page can be scanned:

- The name of the commission, in client words.
- Two or three sentences on the outcome.
- Two sentences on the boundary.
- One line on how to start, and what to send.

Then a photograph of built work that matches that commission, with the constraint named. A services page without the relevant building becomes a brochure. A building without the boundary becomes another homepage.

## Commissions that can carry a heading

You do not need many. Most residential practices can tell the truth with four, and some should stop at two.

A new house. Outcome: a design that can be approved and built, through the stages you include. Boundary: the site types you take, the regions you will visit, whether you require a builder early. Next step: the address, ownership, and a rough brief.

An alteration or extension. Outcome: a clear move for an existing building, usually a plan that respects the fabric and the rules. Boundary: you might not take facades-only decoration, or jobs below a scale where your stage fee still makes sense. Say the scale in plain words if you know it. Next step: the address and what is not working.

An interior. Outcome: rooms, joinery, and materials resolved to the level you actually draw. Boundary: whether loose furniture and styling are in or out. Next step: photographs of the existing rooms and a note on how they live.

Advice before a purchase. Outcome: a short, paid look at whether the site can hold the life they want. Boundary: this is not a free scheme, and it is not a full commission. Next step: the listing and the date they must decide.

If you also take small civic work, a café fit-out, or a multi-unit building, add it only when you want more of it. A heading is an invitation. Do not invite work you will resent.

Drop anything you keep on the page out of politeness. "Masterplanning" with no masterplans. "Sustainability consulting" when you coordinate a specialist and do not sell that service yourself. Honesty here saves the diary.

## Why a capability grid fails

The common failure is a set of tiles: Concept, Detail, Delivery, Research, each with a soft sentence. It reassures the office that the practice looks complete. A client judging taste before competence cannot tell which tile to hire. They already believe you have a process. They came to see if their problem is one you take.

Tiles also hide the boundary. Everything sounds included. The first invoice, or the first meeting, then has to walk it back. That is an expensive way to use a homepage's goodwill.

Replace the grid with the commissions above, even if the page gets shorter. A shorter list that a client can match to their site will outperform a long list that performs range. You can mention the stages inside each commission. Concept, then drawings, then site. That sequence belongs under the offer, not instead of it.

If a partner worries that the page looks small, put the matching projects directly under each offer. Three alterations under "Alterations" is more convincing than eight abstract icons. The work is the proof. The service name is the label.

Check the words against the projects. If the page claims interiors and every photograph is an exterior, fix the page or commission the missing pictures. Do not let the menu get ahead of the archive.

## Boundaries that protect the diary

A boundary is not a rebuff. It is how the right client relaxes. State the ones you already enforce in conversation.

Region. If you will not travel beyond a few hours for site visits, say so. A beautiful page that attracts national inquiries you cannot serve is a tax on the studio.

Scale. If very small cosmetic jobs are the wrong fit, say what you do take. You do not need to publish a minimum fee if the pricing page already has the shape. You do need to stop implying that every shed conversion is welcome.

Role. Architect of the whole house, or interior architect beside another practice, or advisor only. Mixed roles are fine when each one is labeled. A single "we partner with you" line hides the role, and the contract later surprises everyone.

Stage. Some offices prefer to start at feasibility and stay through construction. Some will enter at technical design. Say which. A client with a planning approval already in hand needs to know if you will pick up from here.

Write boundaries as sentences, not as a legal schedule. The agreement can be precise later. The page only has to be true.

## One path into a conversation

Each offer ends on the same action, with different preparation. Do not invent a separate funnel per service, with different button labels, unless the work is genuinely a different product, such as a paid one-day site review with a public price. Even then, the label should say what they get.

Keep the form short. Name, email, the type of commission, and a place to paste the address or the listing. The pricing page, if you have one, can hold the fee shape so this page does not repeat a table. Link to it in one clause. Do not make them hunt.

If the list is still a fog of capabilities and you want a second pair of eyes before rewriting it, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current page and two projects you are proud of. The useful half hour sorts which offers are real, which boundaries you already believe, and what the first screen of each offer should say. Hanabi designs and builds the site after that kind of decision. The call does not need to settle the drawings.

On the build, keep the offers as editable text. Practices change what they take. A services page trapped in a picture of a menu will go stale the season you stop doing fit-outs. Next.js can hold this as ordinary content. The discipline is the writing, not a new plugin for every tile.

## The people behind the offer

A clear list still leaves one question. Who will do this work? Taste can be judged from the projects. Custody cannot. The client wants a name, a role, and a reason this office should be trusted with their particular site.

That is the job of the about page, and it fails when it becomes an origin myth. Read [how an architecture studio should write an about page](/blog/how-an-architecture-studio-should-write-an-about-page) once the offers are in the client's words. The services tell them what they can hire. The about page tells them who picks up the phone.
